enrichment_selection.note: Statement enrichment previously covered only the prior run's top 20 plus five challengers, so a name outside that set could never acquire the metrics that would let it out-rank an incumbent. A rotation of statement-starved names now joins every refresh, plus two dedicated expansion queues sized independently: one for non-financial/non-real-estate names, one for bank/insurer/REIT names -- so financial and real-estate coverage grows on its own deliberate schedule instead of being left to whatever the small, unfiltered rotation happens to reach.

modifiers._comment: Bounded adjustments applied after the evidence blend. They refine, never replace, the evidence score. Units are score points.

macro_regime._comment: FRED-derived context is a sector-sensitive modifier, never a primary ranking factor.

insider_activity._comment: SEC Form 4 open-market activity scored via the Cohen-Malloy-Pomorski (JF 2012) routine-versus-opportunistic split. Routine calendar-scheduled trades score zero - the paper finds their returns are essentially zero. Opportunistic cluster buys earn up to max_points and decay over one to three months, the horizon the effect pays off over. Sells are capped lower because insiders sell for many non-informative reasons.

customer_concentration_risk._comment: ASC 280 customer concentration read from dimensional XBRL (pipeline/concentration_risk.py) - a known, penalty-only risk, not a bet on direction. Below warning_share scores zero; at or above it, half the max penalty; at or above severe_share, the full penalty. SHADOW MODE ONLY (apply_challenger_modifiers, not apply_modifiers) until ConcentrationRiskPercentage1 tagging coverage across the scored universe is measured on a live run - see capability_status.customer_concentration_risk.

geographic_concentration._comment: Single-country revenue concentration read from dimensional XBRL (pipeline/geographic_exposure.py), same shape as customer_concentration_risk. Only fires on concentration in one non-domestic geography, not on international revenue in general. SHADOW MODE ONLY (apply_challenger_modifiers, not apply_modifiers): geographic revenue tags often reflect shipping destination or contracting entity rather than end demand and need spot-checking - see capability_status.fx_exposure.

institutional_13f._comment: Breadth of curated, publicly traded, style=active-only asset managers' quarter-over-quarter 13F position change (pipeline/institutional_ownership.py, pipeline/build_institutional_screen.py). Two-sided like insider_activity: requires min_managers net movers on one side before it scores anything. half_life_days/max_age_days decay the magnitude by how stale the underlying filing already is - a 13F position is disclosed up to 45 days after quarter-end, so it is never fully current; a filing older than max_age_days scores zero rather than being read as still-current. Read from the monthly-refreshed published screen, not fetched live per advisor run.

congressional_buying._comment: Disclosed Congressional stock purchases (pipeline/congress_signal.py), reward-only. Explicit, scoped exception to the 'no political inputs' principle stated in advisor_engine.py's module docstring - see that docstring and TODO.md for what was declined (scoring congressional holdings as evidence a stock/sector is politically protected from failure) versus what shipped (breadth x freshness of disclosed purchases, with a bonus for EXTRAORDINARY_BUY: a member's first-ever trade in a sub-$2B company). Reads the weekly-published congress screen, not a live fetch. Evidentiary basis: Ziobrowski et al. (JFQA 2004, and the 2011 House companion study) find abnormal returns to disclosed Congressional purchases in pre-STOCK-Act samples; whether that survives the post-2012 mandatory-disclosure regime is untested here.

filing_8k._comment: 8-K Item-code materiality (pipeline/edgar_filing_signals.py), classified from SEC's own item taxonomy - never parsed from filing text. Penalty-only: bankruptcy, restatement, delisting, impairment, accelerated debt, exit costs, auditor change, and dilutive unregistered sales each carry a documented negative reading; nothing on Form 8-K is scored positive, since no item code reliably means good news the way these reliably mean bad. Only the single freshest qualifying filing is scored. Reads the 3-day-published SEC filings screen, not a live fetch.

proxy_signal._comment: Contested proxy elections (DEFC14A form code, pipeline/edgar_filing_signals.py) - an unambiguous governance conflict. Penalty-only. Additional soliciting material (DEFA14A) is published as a flag but never scored: the form code alone can't separate a genuine activist situation from routine solicitation updates. Reads the 3-day-published SEC filings screen, not a live fetch.

filing_integrity._comment: Late 10-K/10-Q notification (NT 10-K/NT 10-Q form code, pipeline/edgar_filing_signals.py) - a well-documented distress or accounting-problem signal on its own. Penalty-only; an on-time 10-K/10-Q carries no score signal by itself. Reads the 3-day-published SEC filings screen, not a live fetch.

position_risk._comment: Position decisions reference the highest observed close since purchase. Cost basis remains display-only.

acceleration._comment: Portfolio-level acceleration against the benchmark (src/lib/portfolioAcceleration.js): beta-adjusted excess return over the most recent leg_days, less the same over the leg_days before it, divided by the portfolio's own tracking noise. Beta-adjusting is what separates a portfolio that outran the index from one the index carried; dividing by tracking noise makes the reading comparable across a concentrated book and a diversified one. leg_days is a calendar quarter rather than 63 trading sessions because the portfolio value series is not guaranteed to be daily. skip_days drops the last week, where short-term reversal lives. Same measure as market_behavior.relative_acceleration, which does this per company on daily closes.

benchmark_comparison._comment: Up/down capture and batting average (src/lib/portfolioBenchmarkComparison.js). Capture splits the record by which way the index went, because a single blended ratio cannot distinguish a portfolio that wins by keeping up in rallies from one that wins by losing less in selloffs - opposite portfolios with the same Sharpe. Batting average is bucketed by calendar month rather than by observation: a hit rate is meaningless without a stated cadence, and monthly makes it independent of how densely the value series happens to be sampled.

short_term_view._comment: Fast benchmark-relative reads (src/lib/portfolioShortTermView.js) for the horizons the quarter- and year-scale measures cannot speak to, and for accounts too new for them. Short windows are mostly noise, so every window is published beside a noise floor - one standard error of this portfolio's own tracking noise over a window of that length - and a reading inside the floor is labelled as such rather than reported as a result. Windows report independently: three weeks of history answers the week and honestly declines the month. Beta for the adjustment is fitted over baseline_days rather than the short window itself, so a one-week reading is not adjusted by a one-week beta; below minimum_intervals_for_beta the excess falls back to a plain difference and says so.

shortTermExcessPct._comment: Deliberately wide. A short-horizon excess return is mostly noise, and colouring a +0.4% week green would tell the reader it means something. The tile only takes a tone once the move clears its own noise floor, and these bounds keep even that conservative.

longestUnderwaterDays._comment: Fewer days underwater is better, and tone bounds are read as higher-is-better, so the tile passes the negated day count as its tone value: two months or less underwater reads good, nine months or more reads bad. Up and down capture carry no bounds on purpose - neither is good or bad without the other half, which is what captureSpread scores.

portfolio_analytics._comment: Modified Dietz weights settled external flows by time invested. Correlation analytics use trailing daily total-price returns. The diversification score gives half its weight to effective bets and the diversification ratio, with the other half calibrated from HHI concentration. Performance metric tones use configured good minimums and bad maximums. Values between those boundaries remain neutral, and drawdowns are better when they are closer to zero.

news_intelligence._comment: News remains a 4% tilt. Articles are filtered by entity confidence, deduplicated by title similarity, and weighted by exponential recency, source quality, and whether the item is a source-of-record filing or commentary.

event_type_markers._comment: Keyword classification (brief section 15) -- deterministic and title/source-based, same approach as content_type/source_quality above. A headline can match multiple types; classify_event_type returns every match, ordered by this dict's key order, so the caller decides how to prioritize rather than this function silently picking one.

methodology.principle: Fundamentals lead. Price behavior and news modify confidence; they do not replace business quality.

evidence.valuation: EV/EBITDA and EV/EBIT carry the valuation bucket (Loughran & Wellman's enterprise-multiple factor; Gray & Vogel's multiples comparison). PEG is a minor sanity check because it ignores the time value of money, risk, and cost of capital.
evidence.profitability: Gross profits-to-assets added per Novy-Marx (JFE 2013), which finds it roughly as predictive as book-to-market and complementary to it.
evidence.accounting_quality: Accruals down-weighted and Piotroski raised: the accruals anomaly has decayed in US data since 2002 while the F-score still validates.
evidence.market_behavior: 12-1 momentum (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993) plus Sharpe/Sortino and a low-beta reward (Frazzini & Pedersen 2014), using the same functions as the ETF model.
evidence.news_sentiment: Weighted as a 4% tilt using recency decay, source quality, source-of-record filing labels, entity confidence, and title-level novelty.
evidence.insider_activity: Form 4 trades split routine vs opportunistic per Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski (JF 2012); only opportunistic cluster activity scores.
evidence.caveat: Published factor premia are historical in-sample estimates. They indicate which signals have mattered, not what any of them will return next.

themes.thesis: Howmet was a mature, unglamorous industrial name before a narrow-body production ramp collided with superalloy forging/casting capacity that airlines and OEMs cannot simply order more of - qualifying a new forge for a flight-critical part takes years, not quarters. The move outperformed the broader market by roughly 2.5x over the trailing year with no AI-datacenter linkage at all, and the SpaceX in-house-production episode is a live, dated example of exactly the disconfirming case this theme's guardrails exist to catch rather than ignore.

chain.root_driver: Boeing and Airbus have spent 2025-2026 ramping narrow-body build rates back toward and past pre-2019-MAX-grounding levels, while the specialized superalloy forging and casting capacity that shapes titanium and nickel structural and engine parts was never rebuilt to match - a decade of underinvestment meeting a demand ramp, the same shape as the semicap and memory bottlenecks but with a physical furnace and forge press as the constraint instead of a fab or a laser line.
chain.first_order: The forging and casting houses whose capacity is the pacing item for both airframe structural parts and jet-engine turbine components - dominated by a small number of qualified suppliers because requalifying a new forge for a flight-critical part takes years.
chain.second_order: Downstream machining, aftermarket parts, and engine-component suppliers whose volumes move with the same build-rate ramp, one step closer to the finished aircraft or engine.
chain.disconfirming: Boeing/Airbus build-rate guidance cut (as happened repeatedly post-MAX); an OEM qualifying in-house or alternate production that bypasses the incumbent forger - Howmet dropped roughly 20% in one session in 2026 on news that SpaceX was bringing turbine-blade production in-house, a direct demonstration that this moat is not unlimited; a broader narrow-body demand air pocket (recession, fuel-price spike) that pushes airlines to defer deliveries.

themes.thesis: The most predictable demand curve available: the population that consumes the most healthcare is already born and already counted. What is uncertain is not the demand but who is paid for meeting it, since the same demographics that create the volume also strain the payers - so this theme is scoped to the companies that supply care capacity rather than the insurers who bear its cost.

chain.root_driver: The over-65 share of the population rises for another two decades in every developed market, and healthcare consumption per person rises steeply with age while the clinical workforce does not grow with it.
chain.first_order: Procedure volume: the device makers, orthopedic and cardiovascular implants, and the facilities where those procedures happen.
chain.second_order: Diagnostics and imaging that route patients into procedures, the consumables and sterilization behind each one, and the software that lets a constrained workforce carry more volume per clinician.
chain.disconfirming: Procedure volume growth normalizing after the post-pandemic catch-up rather than continuing; reimbursement rates cut faster than volume grows; hospital capital budgets tightening; staffing shortages capping throughput regardless of demand.

verdict.label: broadening
verdict.summary: The group is outperforming, most of its members are participating, and it is not yet priced as an expensive third of the market.

themes.thesis: A multi-year capex cycle in AI compute pulls through demand for accelerators, HBM/DRAM/NAND memory, networking silicon, and grid and data-center power. The exposure worth identifying is upstream of the spending, not downstream of the share price that has already responded to it.

chain.root_driver: Training and serving large models turns compute into a capital expenditure rather than a software cost, so a handful of buyers commit multi-year budgets to buildings, silicon and power ahead of the revenue those models earn.
chain.first_order: Accelerators, high-bandwidth memory and the networking silicon that lashes them together - the parts of the spend specified by the model rather than by the building.
chain.second_order: Everything the building needs before a chip can run in it: power distribution and conversion, thermal management, the contractors who build the halls, and the generation and grid capacity that has to exist first.
chain.disconfirming: Hyperscaler capex guidance cut or deferred; memory pricing rolling over on oversupply rather than demand; equipment lead times shortening; the buildout concentrating in a single customer whose own spending is slowing.

themes.thesis: The 800G-to-1.6T transceiver transition created a hard manufacturing bottleneck - EML laser yield, not demand - that left even a mid-cap component maker (Lumentum) sold out on capacity through 2027-2028 and produced one of the single largest trailing-12-month returns in the entire US market from a name most investors had written off after the 2022-2023 telecom-spending downturn. Order backlog at these transceiver and connectivity makers is a cleaner, earlier read on whether the AI buildout is real than the accelerator names themselves, which have priced this exposure for years.

chain.root_driver: Training and serving large models at hyperscaler scale requires lashing tens of thousands of accelerators together with enough bandwidth that copper interconnect runs out of reach past a few meters, forcing a wholesale shift from copper to optical links inside and between racks.
chain.first_order: Makers of the pluggable optical transceivers themselves and the components inside them - most acutely the EML (electro-absorption modulated laser) chips whose yields have not kept pace with the 800G-to-1.6T transition, making the laser the physical pacing item for how many transceivers can actually ship.
chain.second_order: Fiber, connectivity, and packaging suppliers into that same buildout, plus the networking-silicon and active-electrical-cable makers that sit at the board edge doing the same bandwidth job at shorter reach.
chain.disconfirming: Hyperscaler capex guidance cut or deferred; transceiver order books shortening rather than extending past 2027-2028; a laser-yield breakthrough (silicon photonics or a new EML process) that removes the scarcity; co-packaged optics reaching volume production and disintermediating pluggable-transceiver demand rather than adding to it.

themes.thesis: The cleanest structural chain that owes nothing to AI enthusiasm: labor is scarce and expensive in exactly the places manufacturing and logistics are being rebuilt, and the substitution is bought as equipment rather than hired. What makes it durable is that the payback is arithmetic - a wage bill against a machine price - so the spending survives the sentiment cycle that thematic screens usually mistake for a trend.

chain.root_driver: Working-age population growth has stalled in every large manufacturing economy while wages in warehousing and assembly keep rising, so output per worker has to come from capital rather than headcount.
chain.first_order: Robots, motion control and machine vision - the equipment that directly replaces a task, bought against a payback period rather than a forecast.
chain.second_order: The sensors, drives, controllers and precision components inside those machines, the industrial software that schedules them, and the integrators who install them.
chain.disconfirming: Machine tool and robot order books turning down; wage growth in logistics and assembly decelerating, which removes the payback; capex guidance from automotive and warehousing customers being cut; integrators reporting project deferrals rather than backlog.

themes.thesis: A battery storage backlog is a contracted interconnection commitment, not an announcement - which is why this theme weights order backlog more heavily than most others in the screen: it is the most direct evidence that a project has cleared the queue rather than merely entered it.

chain.root_driver: Grid-scale storage is the buffer that lets intermittent generation and firm demand clear the same interconnection queue as thermal and nuclear capacity, so it is funded by the same load-growth pressure driving the rest of the electrification buildout rather than by climate policy alone.
chain.first_order: Utility-scale battery energy storage system integrators, whose order backlog is the earliest evidence of contracted, not merely announced, storage capacity.
chain.second_order: The power-electronics and enclosure suppliers into those systems, and the regulated utilities whose capital plans and interconnection agreements fund the buildout.
chain.disconfirming: Interconnection queues clearing faster than new storage requests arrive; utility storage procurement targets missed rather than raised; backlog-to-revenue conversion stalling while backlog itself keeps growing, the same warning this screen watches for in other themes.

themes.thesis: This buildout has failed before on the same mechanism every time: a dominant producer undercuts new domestic capacity on price before it reaches scale. What is different this round is that offtake and price-floor agreements are increasingly government-backed rather than spot-price bets, which is why contracted volume and named-customer evidence matter more here than for most themes in this screen.

chain.root_driver: A small number of countries control rare-earth and critical-mineral processing, and export controls on that processing have turned magnet and battery-metal supply into a national- security question with a multi-year, government-backed response rather than a commodity cycle that clears on price alone.
chain.first_order: Domestic and allied miners and separators of rare earths and battery-relevant minerals, increasingly funded by government offtake and price-floor agreements rather than spot pricing alone.
chain.second_order: The magnet, alloy and specialty-chemical processors who turn separated material into a usable input, and the defense and electrification buyers whose named contracts anchor it.
chain.disconfirming: Offtake and price-floor agreements not renewed at expiration; export controls easing rather than tightening; a dominant producer flooding the spot market to undercut new domestic capacity, the tactic that has repeatedly ended prior attempts at this buildout.

themes.thesis: The supplier theme that every other digital theme feeds: each new workload, payment rail and connected device widens the surface someone has to defend, and the budget is non-discretionary in a way most software spending is not. It is also the theme where filing language is least trustworthy - every company on earth writes about protecting its own data - so the keyword list is written to catch vendors and the exclusions to reject the far larger population describing its own risk.

chain.root_driver: Attack surface grows mechanically with cloud adoption, remote access, digital payments and connected devices, while regulation increasingly makes disclosure and control a legal obligation rather than a technical preference.
chain.first_order: The platform vendors: identity, endpoint, network and cloud security sold as recurring subscriptions.
chain.second_order: The consultancies and managed providers who operate it for firms without a security team, and the network and appliance makers whose hardware enforces it.
chain.disconfirming: Net revenue retention falling as customers consolidate onto fewer platforms; billings growth decelerating faster than revenue; enterprise security budgets being folded into a shrinking overall IT line; breach disclosures no longer producing budget responses.

themes.thesis: Liquid cooling changed from an option to a rack-density specification, which makes attach rate the thing worth measuring rather than the presence of a "cooling" segment: a vendor with a legacy air-cooling or automotive-thermal business looks similar on a keyword screen to one whose growth is entirely in liquid cooling for accelerators, and only segment and backlog evidence tells them apart.

chain.root_driver: Accelerator rack density has moved past what air cooling can remove, so liquid cooling has gone from an option to a specification for the newest accelerator generations - a physical constraint on the AI buildout, not a preference.
chain.first_order: The thermal-management and power-quality vendors data-center operators specify directly: liquid cooling loops, coolant distribution units, and the power gear that shares the rack.
chain.second_order: Heat-exchange and thermal component suppliers, and the contractors who retrofit or build halls to the new cooling specification.
chain.disconfirming: Accelerator generations reverting to air-cooled designs; hyperscaler cooling capex guidance cut; liquid-cooling attach rates flattening in disclosed data-center wins; a shift to lower-density inference-only buildouts that do not need it.

themes.thesis: Allied inventories of guided weapons and air defense interceptors have been drawn down faster than the industrial base can replace them, and the response is multi-year procurement rather than single-year orders. chain.root_driver: Allied inventories of guided weapons and interceptors have been drawn down faster than the industrial base can replace them, and the political response is multi-year procurement rather than annual orders - a budget commitment that outlives an election.
chain.first_order: The primes holding the programs: missiles and munitions, combat aircraft, shipbuilding, and the mission systems that go in them.
chain.second_order: Propulsion, guidance and sensors; the specialty electronics and machined structures the primes buy; and the services firms holding the classified integration work.
chain.disconfirming: Appropriations slipping or being rescinded rather than authorized; primes citing capacity rather than demand as the constraint on guidance; backlog conversion stalling while backlog itself keeps growing; a ceasefire that removes the replenishment case.

themes.thesis: Cash displacement is a decades-long substitution that compounds quietly: every transaction that moves onto a card or an account-to-account rail becomes a metered event for the network carrying it. The economics belong to the toll collectors rather than the banks, which is why this theme is scoped to networks, processors and software rather than to lenders whose earnings turn on credit and rates.

chain.root_driver: Cash and cheque volume keeps converting to electronic payment, and commerce, payroll and billing increasingly embed a payment step inside software rather than beside it.
chain.first_order: The networks and processors that clear the transaction and price it per event.
chain.second_order: Fraud, identity and risk systems that make the rails usable at scale; the core banking and issuer-processing software beneath them; and the terminal and hardware makers at the point of sale.
chain.disconfirming: Payment volume growth converging on nominal consumption growth, which means the substitution is finished; take rates compressing under regulatory caps or account-to- account rails that bypass the networks; consumer credit deteriorating enough to shrink transaction volume itself.

themes.thesis: Reliability and sovereignty have displaced cost as the first question asked of an energy system. That favors what can be dispatched on demand and sourced domestically - gas infrastructure, LNG export, nuclear - and it is a different bet from the decarbonization theme it is routinely confused with, which is why the two are not merged here.

chain.root_driver: Governments and large buyers now price the risk of an interrupted or foreign-controlled supply, and simultaneous load growth means firm, dispatchable capacity is scarce for the first time in a generation.
chain.first_order: The producers and generators themselves: gas and oil operators, independent power producers, and nuclear operators selling into long-dated contracts.
chain.second_order: Pipelines, liquefaction and storage; the drilling, completion and equipment supply chain; turbines and reactor components; and the fuel cycle behind them.
chain.disconfirming: Long-dated LNG offtake contracts failing to renew; permitting reform stalling; power prices falling on new supply rather than weak demand; capital discipline breaking down into a drilling boom, which historically ends this trade rather than extends it.

The money moves in a fixed order - transformers, switchgear, conductor and substation work are ordered years before the generation they connect - so the exposure worth identifying sits with the equipment makers and the contractors doing the interconnection work, not with the utility whose rate base grows at the end of it.

chain.root_driver: Electricity demand is growing again after two decades of flat load, from data centers, reshored manufacturing, EV charging and electrified heating at once, against a network planned for none of it.
chain.first_order: The utilities and independent power producers whose rate base and generation have to expand, and who set the spending everything downstream depends on.
chain.second_order: Transformers, switchgear and medium-voltage gear; the transmission and substation contractors; the conductor, poles and structures; and the distributors who hold the inventory when lead times stretch.
chain.disconfirming: Utility capex guidance flattening; interconnection queues clearing faster than new requests arrive; transformer and switchgear lead times normalizing; rate cases denied, which is where a regulated buildout actually stops.

themes.thesis: Siemens Energy's Grid Technologies segment reported a record EUR51 billion backlog in August 2026 with book-to-bill of 1.48, and will not add its planned +50% transformer/GIS capacity until 2030 - a multi-year gap between order growth and new supply that is technology-agnostic (utilities, renewables, and data centers order the identical equipment) rather than a single-buyer story, which is what makes it durable enough for a systematic screen rather than a diligence note.

chain.root_driver: More than half of the roughly 40 million US distribution transformers are past their service life, while utility grid hardening, renewables interconnection, EV/building electrification, industrial reshoring, and data-center buildout all compete for the same finite large-power-transformer, generator-step-up-unit, and switchgear capacity at once - a multi-buyer demand shock hitting equipment with multi-year lead times.
chain.first_order: Large power transformer, generator step-up unit, and medium/high-voltage switchgear and circuit-breaker manufacturers, whose 2025-2026 lead times ran roughly 125-144 weeks and whose backlogs and book-to-bill ratios are running at multi-year highs.
chain.second_order: Electrical contractors and EPC firms who install this equipment and whose own backlog moves with the same order book, one step downstream of the manufacturer.
chain.disconfirming: Book-to-bill falling back toward or below 1.0; new capacity additions (e.g. Eaton's 2027 South Carolina plant, Siemens Energy's planned +50% transformer/GIS capacity) closing the gap faster than order growth; utility capex guidance cut; a demand-side reversal such as a sharp EV/electrification slowdown removing one of the multiple buyer segments at once.

chain.root_driver: Data-center and reshored-industrial load growth needs firm, round-the-clock power that intermittent generation cannot supply alone, and a hyperscaler signing a multi-year power purchase agreement for existing or restarted nuclear capacity is a buyer of firmness, not of a particular technology.
chain.first_order: Utilities and independent power producers restarting or extending existing reactors, and the enriched-fuel supply chain those reactors and any future small modular reactor fleet both depend on.
chain.second_order: Small modular reactor developers pursuing first-of-a-kind licenses and site work - years from revenue, and the more speculative half of this theme by construction.
chain.disconfirming: Power purchase agreements for restarted capacity not renewed or extended; SMR licensing timelines slipping further rather than holding; HALEU supply bottlenecks easing rather than tightening; data-center operators substituting gas or storage instead of firm nuclear.

themes.thesis: Incretin (GLP-1) demand has outrun the manufacturing that serves it, and the binding constraint is physical - peptide API, sterile fill-finish lines, single-use bioprocessing consumables and injector devices. chain.root_driver: Incretin medicines moved obesity and metabolic disease from a lifestyle question to a treatable one, and demand has outrun the physical capacity to fill and finish an injectable at that scale.
chain.first_order: The franchise owners, whose economics are the most direct expression of the trend and the part already priced as such - which is why they sit in this theme's spender universe rather than its exposure list.
chain.second_order: Peptide API and specialty chemistry, sterile fill-finish and aseptic capacity, the single-use bioprocessing consumables that gate a line, injector devices, and the vials and closures that contain the product.
chain.disconfirming: Fill-finish capacity catching up with demand; an oral formulation displacing injectables and with them the device and containment content; reimbursement narrowing the treated population; the franchise owners insourcing manufacturing they currently contract out.

themes.thesis: The two credible public candidates for this theme (Palo Alto, Fortinet) are both dominated by general enterprise cybersecurity revenue, and the genuine OT/ICS pure-plays (Dragos, Claroty) are private. This theme is declared anyway, with a narrow keyword scope built to exclude the dominant enterprise business, because "no name clears the guardrails on the evidence available" is itself the correct, honest answer this screen should be able to publish rather than lowering the bar to force a pick.

chain.root_driver: Industrial control systems and operational-technology networks were built assuming physical isolation, and connecting them to IT networks and the internet - which the rest of the electrification and reshoring buildout in this screen requires - has removed that isolation faster than purpose-built OT security has been deployed to replace it.
chain.first_order: Security vendors selling into industrial, utility and critical-infrastructure operators specifically, as distinct from the same vendors' much larger general enterprise business.
chain.second_order: Industrial-automation and control-system vendors who embed security into the systems they already sell, rather than selling security as a standalone product.
chain.disconfirming: Named OT/ICS-security revenue flat while overall enterprise-security revenue grows, which would mean this is enterprise cybersecurity discussed in infrastructure language rather than a distinct OT business; a major public pure-play (Dragos, Claroty and similar are private today) never reaching the public market to test that distinction directly.

themes.thesis: Policy and post-2020 supply-chain experience are pulling semiconductor, pharmaceutical and heavy-industrial capacity back onshore. A plant announcement is not the investable event: the spending runs through engineering and construction, process equipment and automation for years before the facility produces anything, and those contractors and equipment makers book it as backlog while the operator books only the capex.

chain.root_driver: Tariffs, subsidy programs and the memory of 2020 have made supply-chain location a board-level risk, so firms and governments are paying a cost premium to hold capacity domestically rather than optimizing purely on unit cost.
chain.first_order: The operators building the plants - fabs, pharmaceutical and battery capacity - whose capex is the money this theme is about.
chain.second_order: Process equipment and materials, the engineering and construction firms who build the shells, the automation that runs them, and the structural inputs they consume.
chain.disconfirming: Announced projects quietly slipping their in-service dates; subsidy disbursement stalling; construction backlogs shrinking; capacity coming online into falling utilization, which turns a buildout into an overhang.

themes.thesis: A fab is committed to years before it produces a wafer, and the equipment order is the first hard evidence of that commitment - well ahead of the accelerator revenue the fab will eventually enable. Order books at the leading equipment makers are the earliest honest read on whether the AI-compute buildout is actually being built, as distinct from whether it is being talked about.

chain.root_driver: Leading-edge fab capacity is the physical constraint under both the AI accelerator buildout and the push for fab sovereignty outside Taiwan, so foundries commit multi-year equipment orders years ahead of the wafers those fabs will produce.
chain.first_order: The equipment makers whose tools are the pacing item for a new or expanded fab - EUV and DUV lithography, etch, deposition and metrology - ordered on lead times measured in years.
chain.second_order: The subsystem and component suppliers into that equipment, and the test and measurement tools that qualify a process node before it ships in volume.
chain.disconfirming: Fab operators pushing out capacity announcements; equipment order books shortening rather than extending; utilization falling at existing leading-edge fabs; export-control relief that removes the sovereignty case for building capacity outside existing hubs.

themes.thesis: A submarine or surface-combatant program is disclosed as remaining performance obligation years before it converts to revenue, which is why this theme reads backlog growth as the earliest honest signal - the same discipline the defense_rearmament theme applies to munitions - rather than treating this as a subset of that broader theme, since drydock and hull-fabrication capacity is a distinct, physically separate constraint from munitions production capacity.

chain.root_driver: Naval shipbuilding capacity has fallen well behind fleet-replacement and allied-order demand, and the policy response - multi-year drydock and submarine-construction investment - is a capacity build, not a one-time order, so it shows up in backlog and capex years before it shows up in delivered hulls.
chain.first_order: The prime shipbuilders holding submarine and surface-combatant programs, whose remaining performance obligation is disclosed years ahead of the revenue it converts to.
chain.second_order: The specialty-metal, sensor and systems suppliers into those hulls, kept a distinct role from the primes since capacity constraints and backlog conversion are read differently at each stage.
chain.disconfirming: Program appropriations slipping or rescinded; primes citing capacity rather than orders as the constraint on delivery; drydock investment plans deferred; backlog growing while delivery schedules keep slipping further out, the sign of a demand problem becoming a capacity problem instead of resolving one.

themes.thesis: Defense and intelligence budgets, not a broad commercial market, are what is actually funding this buildout today - which is why named-customer concentration is read here as confirming evidence rather than as a risk factor the way it would be for a theme with a diversified commercial base.

chain.root_driver: Falling launch cost has turned proliferated small-satellite constellations from a demonstration into deployable national-security and commercial infrastructure, and defense and intelligence buyers are underwriting that shift with multi-year contracts ahead of the broader commercial market catching up.
chain.first_order: Launch providers and small-satellite/autonomous-systems primes whose manifest and program backlog is the earliest evidence of contracted demand.
chain.second_order: Earth-observation and geospatial-data operators who sell the output of that infrastructure as a service, concentrated in defense and intelligence customers rather than a broad commercial base today.
chain.disconfirming: Launch cadence slipping rather than holding; national-security space budgets flat or cut; earth-observation contracts not renewed at expiration; commercial demand failing to diversify beyond the defense and intelligence customer base that funded the buildout.

themes.thesis: Seagate, Western Digital, and SanDisk each traded through 2025 as cyclical, low-multiple hardware names before an AI-driven storage shortage more than doubled all three inside a year (SanDisk's post-spinoff stub alone rose roughly 8x). By August-September 2026 the NAND-heavy names (SanDisk, Micron) had already given back a meaningful share of their summer gains while nearline-HDD-heavy names (Seagate, Western Digital) held up better - a dispersion this theme's per-company signals are meant to distinguish, rather than treating "storage shortage" as one undifferentiated trade.

chain.root_driver: Training-data lakes and inference logging for large models pull hyperscaler storage demand toward both ends of the storage hierarchy at once - more NAND flash for high-performance enterprise SSDs, and more nearline HDD capacity for the bulk, cost-per-terabyte tier - while DRAM/HBM makers simultaneously divert general-purpose NAND and DRAM wafer capacity toward higher-margin AI memory, tightening supply of the "ordinary" storage products this theme is about.
chain.first_order: NAND flash and nearline HDD manufacturers whose capacity is the pacing item: SanDisk (spun off from Western Digital in 2025) and Micron on NAND, Seagate and Western Digital on nearline HDD - each reporting 2026 capacity effectively sold out under long-term contracts.
chain.second_order: Storage controller, interface, and enterprise-SSD component suppliers whose volumes move with the same capacity cycle, one layer down from the finished drive.
chain.disconfirming: Hyperscaler storage capex guidance cut; NAND/DRAM makers reallocating capacity back to general-purpose product as AI-memory (HBM) demand growth slows; nearline HDD unit shipments falling while pricing holds (inventory destocking rather than genuine shortage); new NAND fab capacity coming online faster than guided.

themes.thesis: This is the aging-demographics theme's labor-substitution edge made specific: a robotic surgical system is capital replacing scarce clinician time, not merely capital-intensive care, which is why this theme is kept distinct from the broader aging_demographics screen - the roles overlap by root driver, not by what actually distinguishes the evidence for each.

chain.root_driver: An aging population needing more surgical procedure volume is arriving at the same time as a persistent shortage of trained surgeons and operating-room staff, and robotic-assisted systems substitute capital for that scarce clinical labor rather than merely improving an outcome that unconstrained staffing could already deliver.
chain.first_order: Surgical-robotics platform makers, whose installed base and procedure-volume growth is the direct evidence of clinician-labor substitution.
chain.second_order: Adjacent medical-device makers building robotic and navigation platforms into orthopedic and other procedure lines, and the hospital systems whose capital budgets fund adoption.
chain.disconfirming: Procedure-volume growth slowing at the largest installed base; hospital capital budgets for new system placements cut; competing platforms taking share on price rather than the installed base continuing to expand the total addressable procedure count.

themes.thesis: Three mandates are landing on the same pipes at once - lead service line replacement, enforceable PFAS limits, and reuse in water-stressed regions - on distribution networks already decades past design life. Water utility capex is the funding mechanism and it is rate-recovered rather than discretionary, which makes it one of the few multi-year demand drivers that does not depend on a cycle turning.

chain.root_driver: Three mandates land on the same pipes at once - lead service line replacement, enforceable PFAS limits, and reuse in water-stressed regions - on networks already past design life. Unlike most capex cycles this one is enforced by regulation and recovered through rates, so it does not wait for a cycle to turn.
chain.first_order: Regulated water utilities and the municipal systems whose capital plans fund the work.
chain.second_order: Pumps, valves, meters and filtration; the pipe and hydrants themselves; the engineering firms designing replacement programs; and the treatment chemistry.
chain.disconfirming: Federal and state funding programs lapsing without renewal; PFAS limits weakened or deferred in litigation; utility rate cases denied; municipal budgets deferring replacement schedules, which is how this spending has always been delayed before.

connectivity.methodology: Edge weights are a declared heuristic, not a fitted parameter: two eligible themes sharing one company's exposure score 3.0 (shared root driver), 2.0 (both a supplier/enabler/infrastructure role, different root drivers), 1.5 (one side a labor-scarcity theme the company supplies or enables), or 0.5 (neither - coincidental). connectivity_score sums every pairwise edge among the themes a ticker clears; effective_theme_count first collapses any run of three or more cleared themes sharing a root driver into one effective theme, so a company real in one buildout across several of this screen's themes is not counted as diversified across that many independent drivers.

backlog_growth.source: SEC EDGAR XBRL (dimensional contexts read from the raw filing)
backlog_growth.note: RevenueRemainingPerformanceObligation is XBRL-tagged, not free text - the prior 'filing_parser_required' status was wrong. The blocker was that company_concept/companyfacts return default (non-dimensional) facts only, and filers routinely tag this concept solely in SatisfactionPeriodAxis bands with no undimensioned total for those APIs to see. pipeline.xbrl_dimensions reads contexts out of the filing document directly instead, and EdgarThemeSignals.backlog_values sums the bands when no total exists. Wired into ai_infrastructure.yaml. Per-symbol coverage has not yet been measured on a live production run.

institutional_13f_changes.source: SEC EDGAR Form 13F-HR (curated, publicly traded, style=active managers, via pipeline/build_institutional_screen.py's monthly publish) + OpenFIGI CUSIP mapping
institutional_13f_changes.note: Back in the champion score as a bounded, two-sided modifier ('institutional_13f'), decayed by filing lag rather than treated as current - a 13F position is disclosed up to 45 days after quarter-end, and this reads the monthly screen's own publish date, not today, to compute that lag. Residual bias, not fixed by decay: restricting to publicly traded managers oversamples the largest passive indexers, mitigated (not eliminated) by defaulting to style=active-only managers - see pipeline/config/institutional_managers.json and pipeline/institutional_ownership.py's module docstring. Retroactive amendments (13F-HR/A) are handled explicitly: build_institutional_screen.manager_quarters groups by the period a filing covers rather than filing order, so an amendment supersedes the original it revises instead of being mistaken for a new quarter, and a value change is logged to pipeline/data/institutional_13f/revisions.jsonl rather than silently overwritten. Has never run against the live OpenFIGI endpoint or live 13F filings (no network access existed while this was written); verify CUSIP resolution rate and manager coverage on the first real run.

congressional_buying.source: STOCK Act disclosures via pipeline/build_congress_screen.py's weekly publish (Financial Modeling Prep)
congressional_buying.note: Explicit, scoped exception to advisor_engine.py's 'no political inputs' principle - see that module's docstring. Reward-only modifier ('congressional_buying'): breadth x freshness of disclosed purchases, with a bonus for EXTRAORDINARY_BUY (a member's first-ever trade in a sub-$2B company, build_congress_screen.classify). A request to instead score whether Congress 'wouldn't let a stock/sector fail' was raised and declined - not implemented, see TODO.md. Evidentiary basis (Ziobrowski et al., JFQA 2004) predates the STOCK Act's 2012 disclosure regime; untested against the post-2012 world this reads. Has never run against live FMP data or a live congress screen publish (no network access existed while this was written); verify EXTRAORDINARY_BUY hit rate on the first real run.

fx_exposure.note: Geographic revenue is XBRL-tagged, not free text - the prior 'filing_parser_required' status was wrong for the same reason backlog_growth's was: company_concept/companyfacts return default (non-dimensional) facts only. Scored as single-country revenue concentration (pipeline/geographic_exposure.py) on the same risk-not-direction principle as customer_concentration_risk below, but kept out of the live score ('shadow_only', challenger score_variants only): revenue tagged by geography often reflects shipping destination or contracting entity rather than end demand (a contract manufacturer can book enormous 'China' revenue that is really an assembly step), so this needs spot-checking against real filings, and geographic_tag_coverage above needs measuring, before it penalizes a live score.

customer_concentration_risk.note: ASC 280 customer-concentration percentage read from dimensional XBRL (pipeline/concentration_risk.py), scored as a penalty-only modifier in the champion path as of Phase 3.3. The objection that kept it in shadow mode - that a penalty-only modifier firing only on tagged filers favors whichever companies never tagged the concept - is answered by separating 'filing read, nothing disclosed' from 'no filing read': ASC 280-10-50-42 requires naming any customer at or above 10% of consolidated revenue, so a read filing with no such tag is affirmative evidence of diversified revenue, while an unreadable filing is scored nothing at all. Distinct from the theme layer's customer_concentration_to_spenders: the percentage gives magnitude, not the customer's identity, so it cannot replace that signal's name-matching against confirmed theme spenders.
